name: Theoretical computer science: Spectral graph-lift construction
description: Spectral graph-lift construction under a bounded candidate interface with independent verification; generated mathematical instances, no external dataset.

sources.locator: Interlacing families I: Bipartite Ramanujan graphs of all degrees: signed adjacency and eigenvalues of two-lifts.

evaluation.benchmark: Theoretical computer science: Spectral graph-lift construction
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: sign_edges(graph, budget) -> +/-1 edge signs. graph contains n and ordered undirected edges. Construct connected 3-regular two-lifts of prism graphs; minimize mean spectral radius of signed adjacency (the new eigenvalues), checked independently. budget=32 is the baseline trial budget; all candidates share the 60-second execution ceiling. Numerical spectral ranking does not certify a general theorem.

limitations: This is a bounded native adaptation, not the paper's experimental score or an asymptotic guarantee.
Public development generators can be inspected; independent generalization requires fresh instances after freezing the candidate.

papers.title: Interlacing Families I: Bipartite Ramanujan Graphs of All Degrees
papers.task_relation: The local task searches signings of small prism graphs to minimize a spectral-radius objective. These finite constructions are a restricted instance of the signing problem; they do not prove the paper's infinite-family theorem.
papers.primary_goal: Establish infinite families of bipartite Ramanujan graphs through spectrally controlled graph lifts.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Choose graph-lift edge signs that keep new eigenvalues small and improve expansion.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Constructing graph lifts with strong spectral bounds is central to the cited Ramanujan-graph result.
science_relevance.reason: The source directly studies the spectral construction target. Local finite-instance performance is not presented as a general graph-theoretic result.
